query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a predominantly FCC high-entropy alloy, the formation and retention of short-range chemical order and minor phase precipitates—controlled by post-deformation annealing—govern the balance between partial dislocation/twinning mechanisms at the crack tip, thus determining whether toughness is preserved or degraded under demanding loading conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) in an as-deformed, solution-annealed condition with minimal preexisting short-range order or second phases.
generation.intervention: Vary the post-deformation annealing temperature and time to systematically alter the extent of short-range ordering and any minor phase formation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical fracture toughness testing under engineering-relevant strain rates and temperature ranges typical of structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range chemical order, partial dislocation activity, and possible hcp phase lamellae or fault structures at the crack tip.
generation.mechanism: Altered short-range order modifies interactions of partial dislocations and twinning near the crack tip, enhancing or limiting crack bridging and deflection. Highly ordered or finely precipitated conditions promote dislocation-based toughening mechanisms, whereas disordered or coarsely precipitated conditions lead to reduced crack-tip shielding and lower toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Moderately annealed specimens (fostering beneficial short-range order without excessive second-phase coarsening) will display higher fracture toughness than both under- and over-annealed conditions, which exhibit negligible short-range order or coarse secondary phases, respectively.
generation.baseline: A reference alloy sample solution-annealed under conditions that minimize short-range ordering and second-phase formation before post-deformation treatments.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies primarily to alloys that remain in a single-phase FCC matrix over the annealing range. If extended annealing triggers significant microstructural transformations (e.g., extensive precipitation or transformation to other crystal structures), the toughness may be controlled more by these competing effects than by short-range ordering.
generation.uncertainty: Although multiple studies point to an interplay between short-range ordering and mechanical behavior in high-entropy alloys, direct evidence linking changes in local ordering to macroscale toughness is limited and remains to be fully demonstrated. Confounding influences such as grain-size effects or unaccounted compositional inhomogeneities may obscure the role of local atomic order.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy in a uniformly solution-annealed, deformed state (baseline). Split into multiple batches and apply different post-deformation annealing schedules (e.g., short-time/low-temperature vs. long-time/high-temperature conditions) to create systematic variations in short-range order and minor phases. Conduct standard fracture toughness tests (e.g., KIC or JIC) at relevant engineering strain rates and temperatures on each batch, followed by microstructural and fractographic analysis via TEM/SEM to determine if and how short-range order correlates with crack-tip dislocation activity and branching.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of fracture toughness (e.g., KIC or J at crack initiation).
Chemical order characterization using diffuse scattering or TEM-based nanodiffraction.
Quantification of minor precipitate density and size distributions via SEM/TEM.
Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe dislocation structures, twins, and crack-tip interactions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If varying annealing conditions that significantly alter short-range order and minor phase content does not produce measurable changes in fracture toughness or the expected microstructural mechanisms, the hypothesis that short-range order dominates toughness retention would be invalidated.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) constitute one of the most innovative classes of metallic materials, attracting significant attention from both scientific and industrial communities in recent years [,,]. Their uniqueness lies in the design of chemical composition, where several principal elements are present in nearly equimolar proportions, leading to the formation of high-entropy phases with simplified crystalline structures [,]. These materials exhibit exceptional mechanical, thermal, and corrosion resistance properties, often surpassing those of traditional engineering alloys [,]. HEAs, particularly the Cantor alloy (CoCrFeMnNi), remain among the most recognized and extensively studied representatives within this group []. Since its discovery, the Cantor alloy has attracted significant scientific attention due to its exceptional mechanical properties, distinguishing it from both conventional and other HEAs [,]. It exhibits a single-phase FCC structure with excellent ductility and resistance to brittle fracture, even under cryogenic conditions [,,]. The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys for the design of strong and ductile materials. decision.trend: Early work on single-phase CrMnFeCoNi revealed that a synergy of partial dislocation slip, stacking-fault formation, and twinning promotes excellent ductility and toughness. Subsequent studies showed that tuning metastable phases (e.g., by adjusting hcp precipitation in bcc or fcc matrices) can enhance both strength and ductility through transformation-induced plasticity and twinning mechanisms. More recent findings highlighted the roles of local chemical ordering, edge-dislocation governing flow in refractory alloys, and the formation of 3D defect networks under extreme loading. Despite these advances, the specific interplay among partial dislocations, twinning, phase transformations, and local ordering in sustaining toughness under demanding conditions is still incompletely understood.
decision.unsolved: Although experiments have demonstrated that a mixture of deformation mechanisms can bolster damage tolerance in high-entropy alloys, the exact mechanism dictating toughness retention or loss—particularly under high strain rate or extreme environments—remains unclear. Specifically, it is not fully established how an engineered microstructure (e.g., short-range order, precipitates, and twin boundaries) interacts with evolving dislocation networks to govern crack nucleation and propagation.
decision.lever: Vary the post-deformation annealing temperature and time to modulate ordering and minor phase formation in a single high-entropy alloy composition, then evaluate fracture toughness and in situ crack propagation at relevant loading rates.
decision.why: By regulating heat-treatment conditions (without introducing new alloying elements), one can systematically alter short-range order and any emergent phases, thus revealing how microstructural evolution affects dislocation/twinning interactions and crack-tip processes that control toughness. Comparing these conditions under demanding mechanical testing will verify whether the hypothesized interplay between local ordering, partial dislocation activity, and transformation pathways (fcc-to-hcp) governs toughness. Observing negligible changes in fracture behavior with significantly different microstructures would falsify the proposed mechanism.
